media_work.title: Grace and Justice on Death Row: The Race against Time and Texas to Free an Innocent Man
media_work.focus_or_theme: Wrongful conviction, death penalty, prosecutorial misconduct, attorney-client relationship
media_work.key_statistics: Alfred Dewayne Brown spent over twelve years in prison, including ten years on Texas' death row, for a crime he did not commit

media_item.item_title: Book Content: Grace and Justice on Death Row: The Race against Time and Texas to Free an Innocent Man
media_item.focus_or_theme: Wrongful conviction, death penalty, prosecutorial misconduct, attorney-client relationship
media_item.summary_notes: The book details the legal battle to free Alfred Dewayne Brown from death row, exploring the attorney-client relationship that evolved into a deep brotherhood. It provides a firsthand account of flaws in the criminal justice system, offering a story of hope and redemption.  The foreword is by Sister Helen Prejean.  The book highlights Brown's wrongful conviction for capital murder, focusing on prosecutorial misconduct, withheld evidence, and coerced witness testimony.
media_item.case_details_raw: On April 3, 2003, three men robbed Ace America's Cash Express in Houston, Texas.  During the robbery, store clerk Alfredia Jones (27) and officer Charles Clark (45) were killed. Alfred Brown, Dashan Glaspie, and Elijah Joubert were arrested. Glaspie accepted a plea deal. Brown and Joubert were convicted and sentenced to death. Brown maintained his innocence, claiming he was at his girlfriend's apartment and called her workplace. The prosecution relied on Glaspie's testimony and coerced testimony from Brown's girlfriend.  Exculpatory evidence (phone records) was withheld by prosecutor Dan Rizzo.  In 2014, Brown's conviction was vacated. In 2015, charges were dismissed. In 2019, Brown was declared "actually innocent". In 2020, he was to be compensated for wrongful imprisonment.
key_quotes_raw: What is worse than having a client on Death Row in Texas? Having a client on Death Row in Texas who is innocent and not knowing if you will be able to stop his execution in time.

The book chronicles Brown's extraordinary journey to freedom against very long odds, overcoming unscrupulous prosecutors, corrupt police, inadequate defense counsel, and a broken criminal justice system.
Grace and Justice on Death Row tells the story of such courage and of redemption for Alfred Dewayne Brown, who, like me, is an innocent man.
systemic_issues_raw: Prosecutorial misconduct and withholding of exculpatory evidence
Coercion of witnesses by prosecutors and grand jurors
Inadequate defense counsel during initial trials
Overreliance on testimony from co-defendants who receive plea deals
Racial bias in the criminal justice system
Structural barriers to proving innocence after conviction
The danger of executing innocent people in capital cases
The lengthy and difficult process of exoneration even when evidence of innocence exists
policy_recommendations_raw: Stronger enforcement of Brady disclosure requirements for prosecutors
Reforms to grand jury procedures to prevent intimidation of witnesses
Improved funding and resources for public defenders
Greater accountability for prosecutors who engage in misconduct
Reforms to compensation systems for exonerees
Reconsideration of the death penalty given the risk of executing innocent people

research_notes_raw:
The book not only details the legal battle to free an innocent man from death row but also explores how the attorney-client relationship between Stolarz and Brown evolved into a deep brotherhood. It provides a powerful firsthand account of the flaws in the criminal justice system while also offering a story of hope, perseverance, and redemption.

The foreword is written by Sister Helen Prejean, author of "Dead Man Walking," adding context about the broader issues of capital punishment and wrongful convictions.
